title: How to Stop News Anxiety Without Tuning Out of the World

copy.cover_headline: Your jaw is tight from the headlines

points.headline: The news isn't the problem. The feed is.
points.body: A headline feed has no beginning, middle, or end. Threat after threat, context stripped away, and nothing ever signals that the danger has passed.

points.headline: Why you keep checking
points.body: Checking feels like it will settle the threat. Researchers call it a vicious cycle: more news to ease the alarm, which keeps the alarm going.

points.headline: A 60-second mid-scroll reset
points.body: Unclench your teeth, drop your shoulders. Take 3 to 5 breaths: in through your nose for 4, out gently for 6. Then choose: keep reading, read one full article, or close the app.

points.headline: What it should feel like
points.body: By the third or fourth slow exhale, your shoulders settle and your breath moves lower. The urgency softens enough to think instead of react. Dizzy? Stop and breathe normally.

points.headline: Give the news a finish line
points.body: Set two or three check-in times, turn off breaking-news alerts, and swap the endless feed for a newsletter or front page that has a last item.

reel_lines: The headlines keep coming. Your jaw tightens.
Your breath goes short and high.
A longer exhale brings you back down.

copy.facebook_message:
Staying informed isn't the problem. The endless headline feed is: threat after threat with no context and no ending, so your body stays on alert long after you have the facts.

Mid-scroll, unclench your teeth, let your shoulders drop, and take 3 to 5 slow breaths: in through your nose for 4, out gently for 6. Then decide on purpose whether to keep reading, read one full article, or close the app.

It also helps to set check-in times, turn off breaking-news alerts, and follow a few sources that actually end.

Read the full guide for why the checking loop happens and what the research does and doesn't show.
